claims.value: Cells per mL = CI_cyano x 10^8, termed Microcystis-equivalent cells; developed for Microcystis (Wynne et al. 2010), validated for total cyanobacteria cells in eight eastern states (Clark et al. 2017, Lunetta et al. 2015); MAPE 28.6%
claims.note: Reference 11 is Wynne, Stumpf, Tomlinson, Dyble (2010) Limnol. Oceanogr. 55:2025-2036; 15 is Clark et al. (2017) Ecol. Indic. 80:84-95; 41 is Lunetta et al. (2015) RSE 157:24-34 (ref-list elements CR11, CR15, CR41). Par28 repeats the factor: 'As noted above, CI-cyano can be converted to Microcystis-equivalent cells by multiplying by the factor 10<sup>8</sup> (cells mL<sup>−1</sup>)<sup>11,15,41</sup>, to provide a more intuitive biomass metric.' The MAPE is Mishra's report of Clark 2017, not checked against Clark 2017 itself (full text not reachable).
claims.quote: For purposes of setting risk thresholds, we applied a relationship between CI and cyanobacterial cell concentration of 10<sup>8</sup> cells mL<sup>−1</sup> per 1 unit of CI-cyano<sup>11</sup>. While the relationship<sup>11</sup> was developed for Microcystis (so we term the value as “Microcystis-equivalent cells”), it was validated by<sup>15,41</sup> for unspecified total cell concentrations of cyanobacteria in eight U.S. eastern states across New England (Connecticut, Massachusetts, Maine, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Vermont), Ohio, and Florida. Mean absolute percent error (MAPE) of 28.6% was reported between field-measured cyanobacteria biomass data (cells mL<sup>−1</sup>) and satellite-derived cell biomass<sup>15</sup>.
claims.locator: Data and Methods > Cyanobacteria estimation algorithm,

claims.value: The 10^8 factor is offered to provide a more intuitive biomass metric; bloom magnitude itself is expressed in dimensionless CI units
claims.note: Supports presenting cells/mL as a derived, secondary display value.
claims.quote: Bloom magnitude was expressed in CI units, which is dimensionless. As noted above, CI-cyano can be converted to Microcystis-equivalent cells by multiplying by the factor 10<sup>8</sup> (cells mL<sup>−1</sup>)<sup>11,15,41</sup>, to provide a more intuitive biomass metric.
claims.locator:
Data and Methods > Annual or seasonal bloom magnitude metric,

(paragraph after Eq. 2)

claims.value: The factor was defined from satellite CI against surface-water Microcystis spp. cell counts in western Lake Erie; applied as CI-cyano x 10^8 'as described in Lunetta et al. (2015)'
claims.note: EPA-led paper (Coffer et al. 2021a). Consistent with Mishra 2019 naming Wynne et al. 2010 as the origin.
claims.quote: The standard CI-cyano product was converted to cyanobacterial abundance, in units of cells/mL, as CI-cyano × 10<sup>8</sup> as described in Lunetta et al. (2015). This conversion factor was defined based on a relationship between the satellite-derived cyanobacterial index and surface water samples of Microcystis spp. cell counts in western Lake Erie.
claims.locator: Data and methods > Satellite observations,

claims.value: The Wynne et al. (2010) CI-to-cell relationship is based on Microcystis, r2 = 0.42 (p<0.001), with a potential to underestimate by as much as a factor of 2
claims.note: Stumpf et al. 2012 is written by NOAA co-authors of Wynne 2010 and cites it as reference [15] (ref id pone.0042444-Wynne1). It is a secondary report of Wynne 2010's statistics, since Wynne 2010 itself returned HTTP 403. MERIS-era CI on Lake Erie, not the CyAN v6 OLCI product.
claims.quote: The relationship between CI and cell concentration reported in [15] is based on Microcystis. The r<sup>2</sup> of 0.42, while highly significant statistically (p<0.001) is probably reduced by the comparison of different spatial scales: pixels against water samples in these highly patchy blooms (Figure 4). Cyanobacteria blooms often have concentrations varying orders of magnitude in the space of a 1-km pixel [25]. However, in the context of this study, the relationship of CI to concentration [15] is sufficiently accurate, although with a potential to underestimate as much as a factor of 2.
claims.locator: Methods > Satellite, paragraph beginning 'Blooms in Lake Erie in summer are predominately Microcystis'

claims.value: CI 0.001 corresponds to about 10^5 cells/mL (Wynne 2010), with a conversion uncertainty of about two-fold
claims.note: Same scale as the 10^8 factor (0.001 x 10^8 = 10^5). Secondary report of Wynne 2010 by its co-authors.
claims.quote: A CI of 0.001 corresponds to a concentration of about 10<sup>5</sup> cells mL<sup>−1</sup> [15] ... Current uncertainty in the conversion of CI to cell concentration of about two-fold means that a bloom of CI = 1.0 could contain up to 84 m.tons P.
claims.locator: Methods > Bloom Phosphorus Calculation

claims.value: Satellite cell estimates are expected to differ from field point counts by more than 30%; the relationship is an added uncertainty when scaled to CONUS lakes; spatial patchiness can reach two orders of magnitude
claims.note: Mishra 2019 Discussion. Names manual cell-count error (20-30% or more) and bloom patchiness as sources.
claims.quote: Another source of uncertainty could come from the use of the CI-cyanobacteria cell count relationship when the analysis would be scaled up to the CONUS lakes. ... Similarly, variability in the spatial distribution of biomass in a bloom can add up to two orders of magnitude difference in biomass, as observed by<sup>59</sup> in a cyanobacteria bloom in the Gulf of Finland. ... Therefore, after considering errors from multiple sources, it is expected to have greater than 30% error or difference in satellite estimates, when compared with field measured cell density from a point source in a bloom event.
claims.locator: Discussion,

claims.value: MERIS-derived cell counts were robust for Low (10,000-109,000; about 90%) and Very High (>1,000,000; about 83%) ranges, substandard for 110,000-299,000 (about 28%) and 300,000-1,000,000 (about 40%); confusion attributed to missing taxonomic data needed to convert cell counts to cell volumes
claims.note: Abstract text as shown on the EPA Science Inventory record (Description field). The journal full text returned HTTP 403 in the earlier probe and is closed access per OpenAlex. MERIS era, eight eastern states, 2009-2012.
claims.quote: Results indicated that MERIS provided robust estimates for Low (10,000–109,000 cells/mL) and Very High (>1,000,000 cells/mL) cell enumeration ranges (approximately 90% and 83%, respectively). However, the results for two intermediate ranges (110,000–299,000 and 300,000–1,000,000 cells/mL) were substandard, at approximately 28% and 40%, respectively. The confusion associated with intermediate Cyano cell count ranges was largely attributed to the lack of available Cyano taxonomic data for the in situ measurements that would have facilitated conversions between cell counts and cell volumes.
claims.locator: Record page, 'Description:' field

claims.value: WHO 2021: cell counts are a weaker biomass indicator than biovolume because cyanobacterial cell sizes differ strongly between species; satellite data may be used if calibrated with occasional toxin analyses
claims.note: Speaks to the species and cell-size dependence of any cells/mL figure.
claims.quote: A measure of biomass is best for triggering action – either biovolume or the concentration of chlorophyll a (the latter needs to be combined with a brief visual assessment by microscopy to check whether this mainly represents cyanobacteria, or whether eukaryotic algae dominate). THis is because of the pronounced differences in the cell sizes of cyanobacterial species. Biovolume (i.e. cells/L multiplied by mean cell volume of the species) provides a much better indication of biomass and thus of toxin concentration than mere cell counts. ... Cell counts can nonetheless continue to be used, as can any other locally convenient indicator of the presence and amount of potentially toxic cyanobacteria (e.g. in situ fluorescence, turbidity, satellite data), provided that such a parameter is calibrated with occasional toxin analyses.
claims.locator: Chapter 5 Harmful algal blooms, printed page 68 (PDF page 92). 'THis' is verbatim

claims.value: The producer's release notes say DN converts to 'an estimated cyanobacteria abundance' but give only the DN-to-CI_cyano formula; no cells/mL factor or citation
claims.note: Absence of a factor confirmed by searching the extracted text for 'cells' (no match).
claims.quote: Digital numbers (DN) can be converted to an estimated cyanobacteria abundance derived from CIcyano. CIcyano = 10**(DN * 0.011714 - 4.1870866)
claims.locator: Page 6 (PDF page 6), top

claims.value: CI_cyano values changed between processing versions: version 5 raised them by 15-20% on average; version 6 slightly reduces high-end values. Any fixed cells/mL factor inherits these shifts
claims.note: Version 6 summary on page 8: 'The changes have minor impact at the low-end and tends to slightly reduces CIcyanovalues at the high-end.'
claims.quote: Version 5 shows on average a 15-20% increase in CIcyano values. This is driven by gain changes (using updated ESA gains)
claims.locator: Version 5 improvements/changes, Summary of Analysis, page 12

claims.value: Chl = 6620(±646) x CI_cyano − 3.07(±5), cyanobacterial chlorophyll-a from CI_cyano, CONUS MERIS match-ups
claims.note: Section 3.4 equation (6) gives the intercept as 3.1 (±5.2) in MathML; Table 1 header gives 3.07(±5). Schaeffer et al. 2024 uses 3.07. An alternative abundance scale that links to the WHO 2021 chlorophyll-a alert levels.
claims.locator: Table 1 header row, Chl<sub>BS</sub> column

claims.value: Suggested CI_cyano uncertainty is 1 x 10^-4, equivalent to 0.66 µg/L chlorophyll-a; with the 10^8 factor that is 10,000 cells/mL
claims.note: The 10,000 cells/mL equivalence is arithmetic (1e-4 x 1e8), not stated by the source. Cites Mishra et al. 2023 and Stumpf et al. 2016, not fetched.
claims.quote: (unitless) was suggested to be 1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> (Mishra et al., 2023; Stumpf et al., 2016) or the equivalent of a chlorophyll-a change equal to 0.66 μg L<sup>−1</sup>.
claims.locator:
Material and methods > Forecast threshold CIcyano uncertainty,

(sentence begins 'The uncertainty in CIcyano', CIcyano in MathML)

claims.value: EPA's CyANWeb guide calls the served values cyanobacteria concentrations and says the delivered product is CI_cyano, which includes chlorophyll-a and phycocyanin in the sensor response
claims.note: Previously marked 'agent' in docs/probes/2026-09-23-cyan-vs-clms-assertions.md; now fetched and quoted.
claims.quote: The data the Cyan system reports are cyanobacteria concentrations. The data products as delivered by USGS/NASA are CI_cyano and include chlorophyll-a and phycocyanin in the response of the OLCI satellite sensors (Coffer et al, 2020, Mishra et al, 2019, Lunetta et al, 2015).
claims.locator: 'Understanding the Data', printed page 22 (PDF page 23)

claims.value: SFEI's FHAB API relates CI to Microcystis sp. cells/mL by a multiplier of 100,000,000, borrowed from NOAA Lake Erie work, not field verified for California
claims.note: SFEI serves NOAA-encoded rasters, not CyAN DNs. Two quotes: reference page and pixel-values page.
claims.quote: Pixel values converted to cyano index, which has a range of 0.00006-0.06. Values are unitless by can be related to estimated Microcystis sp. cell concentration (in cells/mL) by a multiplier of 100,000,000.
claims.locator: Reference page, '# Value type' table, row 'ci'. Pixel-values page, second paragraph: 'These conversions have not be field verified for water bodies in California and are provided only for reference.'

claims.value: California's FHAB program discourages specific cell densities from OLCI imagery; cell conversions not recommended without further validation
claims.note: Secondary state report (SCCWRP 2025). A policy position, not a primary scientific source.
claims.quote: FHAB Monitoring Strategy discourages the use of specific cell densities estimated from OLCI satellite imagery (Smith et al., 2021). While published methods to estimate cyanobacterial cell abundances exist, there are a multitude of associated caveats with the approach that lead to this recommendation, which is continued in this report. Due to the uncertainty associated with cell abundance conversions and limitations of the currently published studies on the topic, cell abundance conversions are generally not recommended for application without additional validation and study.
claims.locator: Section 3.1.3 Cell abundances, printed page 21 (PDF page 32)

claims.value: CI and CI_cyano were developed on Microcystis-dominated Lake Erie; performance of the cell conversion is less understood in mixed cyanobacterial communities
claims.note: Secondary (SCCWRP 2025). Same report also states Lunetta's R2 of 0.87 with n = 579 of 2068 samples retained; that is not checked against Lunetta 2015.
claims.quote: An additional confounding factor is that the CI and later the CIcyano algorithms were developed from observations of Lake Erie which is primarily dominated by Microcystis spp., whereas the lakes used for comparison to CIcyano values in Lunetta et al. (2015) were often mixed assemblages of cyanobacterial taxa (though extensive documentation of community composition was not presented), thus the performance of the cell conversion is less well understood in mixed cyanobacterial communities, which are often documented in California waterbodies.
claims.locator: Section 3.1.3 Cell abundances, printed page 21 (PDF page 32)

claims.value: NASA: DN range corresponds to ~10,000 to 7,000,000 cells/ml
claims.note:
No factor or citation on the page. See discrepancy on the arithmetic. Characters ∗ (U+2217) and − (U+2212) are verbatim.
elements rendered as spaces.
claims.quote: To convert Digital Number (DN) to CI_cyano: CIcyano=10^(DN∗0.011714−4.1870866) That range is ~10,000 to 7,000,000 cells/ml.
claims.locator: Section with heading 'DN Guide', paragraph after the list of DN values

claims.value: Sensor detection limit preliminarily estimated at 10,000-20,000 cells/mL
claims.note: EPA-led paper. The CA report repeats it, citing Coffer et al. 2021a, as 'the best estimate provided by the CyAN project' (section 6.2, printed page 65).
claims.quote: Throughout this study, a bloom detected by satellite imagery is defined as any cyanobacterial abundance that exceeds the detection limit of the sensor, which is preliminarily estimated to be between 10,000 and 20,000 cells/mL.
claims.locator: Data and methods > Satellite observations,

claims.value: DN 1-253 roughly ~10-20,000 to 7,000,000 cells/mL; the conversion is a very rough estimation
claims.note: Secondary (SCCWRP 2025).
claims.quote: DNs of 1 – 253 are roughly equivalent to ~10-20,000 – 7,000,000 cells/mL. It should be noted though that the conversion of CIcyano to cell abundance data is currently a very rough estimation (more details in Chapter 3).
claims.locator: Section 6.2 Detection Limit, printed page 66 (PDF page 77)

claims.value: NOAA's Lake Erie bulletin: estimated threshold of cyanobacteria detection 20,000 cells/mL
claims.note: NOAA's own Lake Erie OLCI product and encoding, not CyAN. Bulletin dated 2026-09-25; the URL is overwritten with each bulletin.
claims.quote: The estimated threshold of cyanobacteria detection is 20,000 cells/mL.
claims.locator: Page 1, caption of the satellite image

claims.note: The abstract names only Low and Very High. The EPA Android app screenshot labels the middle two Medium and High (see categories-epa-android-app-defaults-figure).
claims.quote: Results indicated that MERIS provided robust estimates for Low (10,000–109,000 cells/mL) and Very High (>1,000,000 cells/mL) cell enumeration ranges (approximately 90% and 83%, respectively). However, the results for two intermediate ranges (110,000–299,000 and 300,000–1,000,000 cells/mL) were substandard
claims.locator: Record page, 'Description:' field

claims.value: Low ≤20,000; Moderate 20,000-100,000; High >100,000; added Very High >1,000,000
claims.note: Mishra cites WHO via reference 48, Chorus and Bartram 1999. Very High is Mishra's addition, not WHO's. The area-normalized CI thresholds in the same paragraph are per 0.09 km2 pixel, not per-pixel CI.
claims.quote: Based on the World Health Organization’s (WHO) cell abundance threshold<sup>48</sup>, three magnitude classes were considered for categorizing lakes as Low (≤20,000 cells mL<sup>−1</sup>), Moderate (20,000 ≤ cells mL<sup>−1</sup> ≤ 100,000), and High (>100,000 cells mL<sup>−1</sup>) exposure health risk. ... We have also added ‘Very High’ (V.High) category when estimated cyanobacteria concentration and area-normalized magnitude exceeded 1,000,000 cell mL<sup>−1</sup> and 0.111, respectively.
claims.locator: Data and Methods > Annual or seasonal bloom magnitude metric,

claims.value: WHO 2003: 20,000 cyanobacterial cells/ml (relatively low probability of adverse effects; or 10 µg/L chlorophyll-a with cyanobacterial dominance); 100,000 cells/ml (moderate; about 50 µg/L chlorophyll-a); scum in swimming areas (high)
claims.note: The PDF text layer renders the micro sign as 'm' ('10 mg chlorophyll-a/litre'); the rendered glyph is presumably µ, as Figure 8.1 on PDF page 172 extracts as '50 µg/l chlorophyll-a'. A checker should view the page. Same levels in Chapter 8, section 8.7 and Table 8.3 (PDF pages 182-183, printed 149-150). Coffer et al. 2021b P20 restates them citing WHO 2003.
claims.quote: a guideline level of 20 000 cyanobacterial cells/ml (corresponding to 10 mg chlorophyll-a/litre under conditions of cyanobacterial dominance) can be derived. A level of 100 000 cyanobacterial cells/ml (equivalent to approximately 50 mg chlorophyll-a/litre if cyanobacteria dominate) represents a guideline value for a moderate health alert in recreational waters. The presence of cyanobacterial scum in swimming areas represents the highest risk of adverse health effects
claims.locator: Executive summary, printed page xxvii (PDF page 28)

claims.value: WHO 2021: Vigilance 1-4 mm³/L biovolume or 1-12 µg/L chl-a; Alert Level 1 4-8 mm³/L or 12-24 µg/L chl-a; Alert Level 2 scum or transparency <0.5-1 m (with cyanobacterial dominance)
claims.unit: biovolume mm³/L; chlorophyll-a µg/L; Secchi transparency m
claims.note: No cells/mL thresholds in the 2021 framework. The Fig. 5.1 layout text on PDF page 17 extracts as 'Up to 3-12 µg/L' for vigilance, which differs from the executive-summary '1–12'; not resolved.
claims.quote: Cyanobacterial biomass indicator values (thresholds in Fig. 5.1 alert level framework): • Vigilance level – 1–4 mm³/L biovolume or 1–12 µg/L chlorophyll a (with dominance of cyanobacteria). • Alert Level 1 – 4–8 mm³/L biovolume or 12–24 µg/L chlorophyll a (with dominance of cyanobacteria). • Alert Level 2 – scum or transparency <0.5–1 m.
claims.locator: Executive summary, Chapter 5 box 'Indicators and guideline values', printed page xvii (PDF page 19)

claims.value: WHO 2021's alert level framework replaces the three-tiered 2003 table
claims.note: The 2021 text cites 'Table 8.1 in WHO, 2003'; in the fetched 2003 PDF the guideline table is Table 8.3 and Table 8.1 lists toxins. Cell-count tiers of 20,000 and 100,000 are therefore superseded guidance.
claims.quote: The alert level framework (ALF) given in Fig. 5.1 replaces the three-tiered table given in the 2003 guidelines (Table 8.1 in WHO, 2003).
claims.locator: Chapter 5, printed page 68 (PDF page 92)

claims.value: Clark et al. 2017 ranked lakes by frequency above the WHO high threshold of 100,000 cells/mL
claims.note: Abstract only. The CA report and Coffer 2021b describe Clark 2017's use of 100,000 cells/mL as a demonstration threshold.
claims.quote: Recreational and drinking water sources in Florida and Ohio were ranked from 2008 through 2011 by cyanoHAB frequency above the World Health Organization’s (WHO) high threshold for risk of 100,000 cells mL<sup>−1</sup>.
claims.locator: Abstract

claims.value: CyANWeb bins markers into low, medium, high, very high; the guide says defaults are set to WHO limits; users can change them
claims.note: No numbers in the text. See the figure claim below.
claims.quote: The colors used by pin marker symbology and text are binned into four categories of cyanobacteria concentration: low, medium, high, and very high. The default values for these categories are set to World Health Organization limits.
claims.locator: 'Markers – user configuration settings', printed page 12 (PDF page 12)

claims.value: CyANWeb Figure 7 dialog shows Low to 100000; Medium 100000-300000; High 300000-1000000; Very High higher than 1000000; Alert when higher than 1000000
claims.unit: cells/mL (unit not shown in the dialog; inferred from the app's display unit)
claims.note: Values read visually from the raster screenshot (JPEG, 2545 x 1510 px, PDF page 12). They are not in the PDF text layer, so the quote is the caption only. discrepancies.topic: NASA's stated cells/mL range versus the arithmetic of the DN formula and the 10^8 factor

statements.quote: To convert Digital Number (DN) to CI_cyano: CIcyano=10^(DN∗0.011714−4.1870866) That range is ~10,000 to 7,000,000 cells/ml.
we applied a relationship between CI and cyanobacterial cell concentration of 10<sup>8</sup> cells mL<sup>−1</sup> per 1 unit of CI-cyano<sup>11</sup>
which is preliminarily estimated to be between 10,000 and 20,000 cells/mL

discrepancies.note: Computed with the documented formula and factor: DN 1 gives CI_cyano 6.677708e-05, 6,678 cells/mL. DN 253 gives CI_cyano 5.977993e-02, 5,977,993 cells/mL. 10,000 cells/mL corresponds to DN 15.97 (DN 16 gives 10,008). 7,000,000 cells/mL corresponds to DN 258.85, outside the 1-253 data range. So the page's range is about 1.5 times too high at the low end and about 1.17 times too high at the high end. No fetched source explains it. Two unconfirmed readings: the low end may be the detection-limit estimate of 10,000-20,000 cells/mL rather than DN 1; the high end matches a NOAA-style scaling, 10^(0.012 x code - 4.2) x 10^8 at code 253 = 6,854,882. SFEI's NOAA-encoded table tops out at code 250, >6,327,038. The CA report repeats '~10-20,000 – 7,000,000 cells/mL'. Unresolved.

discrepancies.topic: Sign of the SS(665) phycocyanin test that separates cyanobacteria

statements.quote: In this case, a conditional negative SS (665) value indicates the presence of PC.
Accordingly, when SS (665) < 0, cyanobacteria are presumed absent, and when SS (665) > 0, cyanobacteria are presumed present.
(SS(665); λ- = 620 nm; λ+ = 781 nm) that is sensitive to phycocyanin absorption at 681 nm.

discrepancies.note: Mishra 2019 and Coffer 2020 give opposite signs for cyanobacteria presence. The sign likely depends on whether SS or -SS is reported, but neither paper says so. The CA report follows Coffer 2020 and also gives λ+ = 781 nm and phycocyanin absorption at 681 nm, where Mishra and Coffer give 681 nm and 620 nm. Not needed for the dashboard text. It bears on any sentence that explains how the index separates cyanobacteria.

statements.quote: :units = "CI_stumpf:sr^-1,CI_cyano:sr^-1
Bloom magnitude was expressed in CI units, which is dimensionless.
Values are unitless by can be related to estimated Microcystis sp. cell concentration

discrepancies.note: The binned-file metadata lists inverse steradians. The papers and SFEI call the index dimensionless or unitless. Schaeffer 2024 P19 also says '(unitless)'. The 10^8 factor is stated as cells mL^-1 per unit CI, so the page can present CI as unitless and cells/mL as derived.

discrepancies.topic: Coffer et al. 2020 detection limit 'at or above a CI value of 1'

statements.quote: The minimum detection limit for cyanobacteria is currently estimated to be at or above a CI value of 1. For reference, this corresponds to the World Health Organization (WHO) low-risk threshold
(unitless) was suggested to be 1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> (Mishra et al., 2023; Stumpf et al., 2016)

The page can say the factor is uncertain by up to about a factor of two and is species-dependent.

limitations: Quote rendering from XML and HTML: all tags are removed except <sup> and <sub>, which are kept literally as '<sup>' and '<sub>'. Entities are decoded. No-break space (U+00A0), thin space (U+2009), and hair space (U+200A) become ordinary spaces. Runs of whitespace collapse to one space. In HTML, tags are replaced by a space before collapsing; in XML, tags are removed without a space, so '<xref>' citation numbers inside <sup> join the text. MathML becomes '[MATH]', and no quote spans a [MATH] token.

Quotes from PDFs come from pdftotext (poppler) default-mode text, whitespace collapsed. ' ... ' in a quote joins two verbatim segments from the same locator. Each segment was checked by script as an exact substring of the normalized saved file (49 claims, 0 failures).

The WHO 2003 PDF text layer encodes the micro sign as 'm' in several places ('10 mg chlorophyll-a/litre'). Quotes keep the extracted 'mg'; the rendered page presumably shows µg. Figure 8.1 in the same PDF extracts as 'µg/l'.

The two app-default category claims are figure readings from raster screenshots (PDF page 12 of EPA/600/B-21/072, PDF page 10 of EPA/600/B-19/086). Their numbers are not in any text layer. The quote field holds the adjacent verbatim text. They are proposed as 'probe', not 'documented'.
The CA report (SCCWRP 2025), the SFEI API pages, and Stumpf et al. 2012 on Wynne 2010 are secondary for the statements they relay from WHO, Lunetta, Coffer, or Wynne. The notes say so claim by claim.
The NOAA bulletin URL is overwritten with each new bulletin. The saved copy is the 2026-09-25 bulletin.
The EUMETSAT release notice is an Internet Archive capture, because the live page returns 404.

The arithmetic in the discrepancy notes (DN to CI to cells, thresholds to DN) is computed from the documented formula and factor. It is not a source statement. First CyAN DN at or above each threshold: 10,000 cells/mL DN 16; 20,000 DN 42 (20,179); 100,000 DN 102 (101,799); 1,000,000 DN 187 (1,007,932); 12 µg/L chl-a via Seegers DN 132 (228,645 cells/mL-equivalent).
Mishra 2019 and the release notes are byte-identical re-fetches of the repository's existing reference copies. The sha256 values are in sources-manifest.json.

Access times are 2026-09-25 between 16:57 and 17:18 UTC. Every source was fetched with curl and the user agent 'public-water-quality-pipeline/0.1 (research)'. WebSearch was used only to find URLs. No quote comes from a search snippet or from WebFetch.
